title: Impact of Revising Wages for Cleaning Sector on Cleaners and Workers in Other Sectors
what_it_is: Impact of Revising Wages for Cleaning Sector on Cleaners and Workers in Other Sectors

sections.label: Cleaning sector PWM questions
sections.summary: Questions ask the Manpower Minister about cleaning workers' skillsets, viable livelihoods, PWM wage ladder timing, roll-out considerations and industry consultation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) what skillsets has the Ministry planned for workers in the cleaning sector to possess to remain relevant in the move towards cleaning automation; and (b) what is the Ministry’s plan to ensure that the cleaning industry will continue to provide viable livelihoods in the long term.

sentences.speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) why is the wage ladder under the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for the cleaning sector determined only in 2021 when the announcement for a six-year wage increment under the PWM for that sector was made in 2016; (b) what are the considerations for the six-year roll-out period; and (c) whether the cleaning industry has been consulted on wage quantum and rate of increments.

sections.label: Cleaning productivity and PWM coverage
sections.summary: Questions ask about raising cleaning productivity alongside the wage floor doubling, how, unemployment risk, and PWM beneficiary numbers and lessons.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) whether the Government intends to increase labour productivity of the cleaning sector in tandem with the projected doubling of the wage floor from the current $1,236 to $2,420 by 2028 under the latest updates to the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for this sector; (b) if so, how will this doubling of productivity be brought about; and (c) whether workers in this sector will face higher unemployment if this productivity increase cannot be achieved.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Manpower under the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for workers with wages at the bottom 20% of the workforce (a) what is the number and percentage of workers from the cleaning, security, landscape and lift and escalator industries who can benefit; (b) what is the additional number and percentage of workers who will benefit from the expansion of PWM into the food, retail and waste management industries; and (c) what lessons can be drawn from the implementation of the PWM to expedite its expansion.

sections.label: Workfare payouts to low-wage workers
sections.summary: Close to a million low-wage workers have benefited from nearly $7.8 billion in Workfare payouts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: Close to a million low-wage workers have since benefited from nearly $7.8 billion in Workfare payouts.

sections.label: Real wage growth at 20th percentile
sections.summary: From 2009 to 2019, real wages at the 20th percentile grew 39% cumulatively, faster than the median worker's 33%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: To Miss Cheng Li Hui's question, from 2009 to 2019, the real wages at the 20th percentile of our resident workforce grew 39% cumulatively, faster than the median worker at 33%.

sections.label: COVID-19 low-wage earnings support
sections.summary: COVID-19 cut low-wage workers' earnings to $2,340 a month, but WIS and the 2020 Workfare Special Payment mitigated the impact.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: While COVID-19 has resulted in a fall in the earnings of low-wage workers to $2,340 a month, Government schemes such as the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) and the one-off Workfare Special Payment (WSP) in 2020 helped to mitigate this impact.

sections.label: In-house workers into Progressive Wage
sections.summary: In-house cleaning, security and landscaping workers will enter the Progressive Wage system, expanding coverage to up to 218,000 workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: It will also bring in-house cleaning, security and landscaping workers into the Progressive Wage system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: These moves will significantly expand coverage to up to 218,000 workers.

sections.label: Raising cleaners' wages
sections.summary: The TCC collectively wanted to raise cleaners' wages in a sustained manner and revalue their work in the COVID-19 fight.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: The TCC was clear in its collective desire to raise the wages of our cleaners in a sustained manner and revalue the work of our cleaners who have been integral in our fight against COVID-19.

sections.label: TCC recommendations and cleaner training
sections.summary: The TCC is committed to submitting recommendations before year end and has upgraded training requirements for cleaners.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: Notwithstanding the challenging economic conditions, they are committed to submitting their recommendations before the end of the year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: To Ms Yeo's question on re-skilling, the TCC has upgraded the training requirements for cleaners.

sections.label: Tripartite process for PWM
sections.summary: Each PWM is agreed by a tripartite process, giving confidence wage increases are supported and will not risk employment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: Each PWM implemented is agreed by a tripartite process, which gives greater confidence that such wage increases can be supported by the market, by the society and will not put employment at risk.

sections.label: Company survivability and worker employment
sections.summary: PWM negotiations considered both the survivability of companies and the employment outcomes of workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: In fact, this is a very important aspect of our PWM negotiations because one of the key considerations we also had was both the survivability of our companies, as well as, at the same time, the employment outcomes of our workers.

sections.label: Support for challenged sectors
sections.summary: The Tripartite Workgroup will study and roll out recommendations to layer added support for companies transitioning into new PWM wage structures and new sectors.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: We also understand that in the current market, some sectors are a bit challenged and, therefore, these may require further support.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: This is where the Tripartite Workgroup will study and roll out the recommendations soon to see how can we can layer on added support to help companies transition into some of these new PWM wage structures as well as for new sectors coming into PWM.

sections.label: Tripartite consensus as safeguard
sections.summary: Singapore's system is unique in that its safeguard is tripartite consensus, with employers and employees agreeing based on projections and market conditions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: In fact, that is the uniqueness of Singapore's system in that our safeguard is the tripartite consensus, with the employers on board, the employees agreeing, knowing what the projections look like and what they can agree to, and what they see as the market conditions coming forward.

sections.label: Productivity and PWM disemployment
sections.summary: The speaker lacks productivity figures but notes no disemployment was seen in years when PWM was implemented.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: I do not have the figures for productivity with me.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: But I think it is important to also look at productivity from the fact that we did not see disemployment in the years where PWM has been implemented.

sections.label: Employer conversations on blind spots
sections.summary: Close conversations with employers are important to look at where the blind spots are.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: Indeed, this is why close conversations that we have with employers are important, to look at where the blind spots are.

sections.label: Training, unions and job redesign
sections.summary: The speaker wants to work with employers, unions, trade associations and stakeholders on training, job scope and job re-design for worker transition.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: This is something that we want to work on with the employers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: But, at the same time as well, it is inevitable that even without PWM, you might find, because of industry transformation, certain jobs going obsolete.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: That is where the whole training and skills element becomes very important.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: We have to work with the unions, the trade associations and all our stakeholders to see how we can better improve the job scope as well as the job re-design to help workers transition.

sections.label: Labour policies and job creation
sections.summary: Keeping labour policies tight or the economy growing can continue to create more jobs and opportunities for everyone.

sentences.speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
sentences.text: Overall, for as long as we keep our labour policies tight or keep our economy growing, we can then continue to create more jobs and more opportunities for everyone.
